title: Given a Scenario, Implement Identity and Access Management

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Identity and access management answers several different questions: Who are you? How do you prove it? What are you allowed to do? How do we record what you did?
CompTIA separates IAM into secure access methods, authentication, authorization, and accounting.
A useful mental model is: Authentication → Who are you? Authorization → What can you do? Accounting → What did you do?

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: Is this scenario establishing identity, granting permissions, accessing cloud systems, or recording activity?
sections.callout: Prove identity → authentication. Grant rights → authorization. Record actions → accounting.

sections.title: Secure Access to the Cloud Management Environment
paragraphs: The management environment is where administrators or applications control cloud resources. CompTIA includes several ways to access it.

entries.title: Programmatic Access
paragraphs: Programmatic access allows software or scripts to interact with cloud management services without a human clicking through a portal.

entries.title: Application Programming Interface (API)
paragraphs: An API exposes defined operations that software can call. Think: Software talks directly to the cloud service.
entries.recognitionCue: An application directly requests cloud operations → API.

entries.title: Software Development Kit (SDK)
paragraphs: An SDK provides libraries and tools developers can use to build applications that interact with cloud APIs.
Think: Developer toolbox for working with the API.
entries.recognitionCue: Developers need language-specific libraries or tools to access cloud services → SDK.

entries.title: Command-Line Interface (CLI)
paragraphs: A CLI lets administrators manage cloud resources using typed commands.
Think: Cloud administration from the terminal.
entries.recognitionCue: An administrator uses commands or scripts rather than a graphical portal → CLI.

entries.title: Web Portal
paragraphs: A web portal provides browser-based graphical cloud management. Think: Point, click, configure.
entries.recognitionCue: An administrator manages cloud resources through a browser GUI → web portal.

sections.title: Secure Access to Cloud Resources
paragraphs: Managing the cloud environment and connecting to resources inside it are not always the same thing.

entries.title: API
paragraphs: Applications may directly access a cloud resource through its API.
entries.recognitionCue: Application-to-service access → API.

entries.title: Secure Shell (SSH)
paragraphs: SSH provides secure remote command-line access and is commonly associated with administering Linux and Unix-like systems.
Think: Secure remote terminal.
entries.recognitionCue: Encrypted command-line access to a server → SSH.

entries.title: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)
paragraphs: RDP provides graphical remote desktop access and is commonly associated with Windows systems.
Think: Remote Windows desktop.
entries.recognitionCue: A remote graphical Windows session → RDP.

entries.title: Bastion Host
paragraphs: A bastion host is a specially controlled system used as a secure access point into otherwise restricted systems.
Instead of exposing every internal virtual machine directly, administrators first connect to the bastion.
Think: Guarded front door into the protected network.
entries.recognitionCue: A controlled jump point into private cloud resources → bastion host.

entries.title: Local Users
paragraphs: Local users are identities maintained directly within the system or cloud environment. Think: The account lives here.
entries.recognitionCue: The identity is created and managed directly on the target environment → local user.

entries.title: Federation
paragraphs: Federation allows an identity established in one system or organization to be trusted by another.
Think: Prove who you are over there, and we will trust it here.
entries.recognitionCue: Users authenticate through one identity system and gain access to another environment → federation.

entries.title: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML)
paragraphs: SAML exchanges authentication and authorization information between identity systems.
It is strongly associated with enterprise federation and single sign-on. Think: The enterprise identity provider tells the cloud service who you are.
entries.recognitionCue: Enterprise SSO or federation uses identity assertions → SAML.

entries.title: Token-Based Authentication
paragraphs: Token-based authentication uses a token representing an authenticated identity or session.
Instead of repeatedly transmitting a password, the system can use the token. Think: Show the trusted pass.
entries.recognitionCue: Access depends on a generated security token → token-based authentication.

entries.title: Directory-Based Authentication
paragraphs: Directory-based authentication relies on a centralized directory containing user identities and related information.
Think: Central employee identity book.
entries.recognitionCue: Accounts are authenticated against a centralized directory → directory-based authentication.

entries.title: Multifactor Authentication (MFA)
paragraphs: MFA requires more than one authentication factor. Typical categories are something you know, something you have, and something you are.
Think: A password alone is not enough.
entries.recognitionCue: Two or more different authentication factors are required → MFA.

entries.title: OpenID Connect
paragraphs: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer commonly used to authenticate users in modern applications.
Think: Modern application identity and authentication.
entries.recognitionCue: A modern web or application service needs identity information during authentication → OpenID Connect.

sections.title: Authorization Models
paragraphs: After authentication proves identity, authorization determines permissions.

entries.title: Role-Based Access Control
paragraphs: Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions based on a user's role, such as administrator, developer, auditor, or help desk.
Think: Your job role determines your permissions.
entries.recognitionCue: Access is assigned based on job function → RBAC.

entries.title: Group-Based Access Control
paragraphs: Permissions are assigned to groups, and users receive those permissions through group membership.
Think: Join the group → inherit its access.
entries.recognitionCue: Permissions follow group membership → group-based access control.

entries.title: OAuth 2.0
paragraphs: OAuth 2.0 allows a user or application to grant limited access to resources without sharing the user's password with the requesting application.
Think: You can access this resource on my behalf, but only what I authorize.
entries.recognitionCue: One application needs delegated access to another service → OAuth 2.0.

entries.title: Discretionary Access
paragraphs: With discretionary access, the owner of a resource can decide who receives access.
Think: I own it, so I choose who gets in.
entries.recognitionCue: The resource owner determines permissions → discretionary access.

sections.title: Accounting
paragraphs: Accounting tracks activity associated with identities.

entries.title: Audit Trail
paragraphs: An audit trail records actions and events so administrators can determine who performed an action, what was changed, and when it occurred.
Think: Who did what, and when?
entries.recognitionCue: Actions need to be traceable to an identity → audit trail.

sections.title: IAM Recognition Cues
bullets: Developer libraries for cloud interaction → SDK
Identity lives on the system → Local user
One identity provider is trusted elsewhere → Federation
Security token proves a session → Token-based

entries.title: Authentication vs. Authorization
paragraphs: Authentication asks who you are. Authorization asks what you may do.

entries.title: OpenID Connect vs. OAuth 2.0
paragraphs: OpenID Connect provides authentication and identity. OAuth 2.0 provides authorization and delegated access.

entries.title: SAML vs. OAuth
paragraphs: SAML strongly points toward enterprise federation and SSO. OAuth points toward delegated authorization.

entries.title: SSH vs. RDP
paragraphs: SSH provides a remote command line. RDP provides a remote graphical desktop.

entries.title: Bastion Host vs. Direct Access
paragraphs: A bastion host reduces the need to expose every internal system directly.

sections.title: Maestro Recognition Sheet
bullets: Temporary identity or session proof → Token
